questions.q: Why does portfolio variance depend on the full covariance matrix rather than just each asset's individual variance?
options: Because portfolio variance is always equal to the largest individual asset variance
Because the off-diagonal covariance terms capture how assets move together, and two correlated assets held together don't diversify each other away
Because regulators require reporting the full matrix
Individual variances are never used in portfolio variance calculations
questions.explain: Portfolio variance is w'*Sigma*w, a sum over every pair of assets; ignoring off-diagonal covariance terms badly misstates risk for correlated or concentrated portfolios.

questions.q: What happens to the sample covariance matrix when the number of assets N approaches or exceeds the number of observations T?
options: It becomes more accurate
It becomes singular (if T<=N) or very noisy, and cannot be reliably inverted
It automatically shrinks toward a diagonal matrix
Nothing changes; sample size doesn't affect the covariance matrix
questions.explain: Estimating a full N-asset covariance matrix requires N*(N+1)/2 parameters; when observations are scarce relative to assets, the matrix becomes singular or dangerously noisy.

questions.q: How does a factor-model covariance estimate reduce the number of parameters that need to be estimated?
options: By ignoring idiosyncratic risk entirely
By expressing Sigma as B*Sigma_F*B' + D, replacing N*(N+1)/2 free parameters with roughly N*k loadings, a small k x k factor covariance, and N idiosyncratic variances
By assuming all assets have identical returns
By using only the two largest assets in the portfolio
questions.explain: The factor-model decomposition collapses the covariance estimation problem to a much smaller number of parameters tied to k common factors, at the cost of assuming the factor structure fits reality.

questions.q: In the worked example with 150 assets and 100 observations, what was the rank of the sample covariance matrix, and why?
options: Rank 150 (full rank), because sample covariance is always full rank
Rank 99, because with only 100 observations you cannot estimate more than 99 independent directions of variance
Rank 0, because the matrix was entirely zero
Rank 3, matching the number of true factors
questions.explain: With n_obs=100, the sample covariance matrix came out rank 99 -- mechanically singular, since mean-centering plus only 100 observations limits it to at most 99 independent directions.

questions.q: In the worked example, how did the factor-model covariance compare to the sample covariance in mean absolute error versus the true covariance matrix?
options: The factor-model covariance had roughly double the error of the sample covariance
They had identical error
The factor-model covariance had roughly half the error of the sample covariance (0.000049 vs 0.000090), while also being full rank and invertible
The sample covariance had zero error
questions.explain: The factor-model covariance was both full rank (unlike the singular sample covariance) and closer to the true covariance matrix, with mean absolute error of 0.000049 versus the sample covariance's 0.000090.
